passages.text: The argument about objects taken from one country and displayed in another is usually conducted as though a single question were at stake, and it is not. Three quite different disputes are folded into the word restitution, and they have different answers. The first is about theft: an object removed by force, or bought from somebody who had no right to sell it, was taken unlawfully, and the case for returning it does not depend on where it is best looked after. The second is about interpretation: an object acquired legally a century ago may still be exhibited in a way that the descendants of its makers find false, and this is an argument about labels rather than about ownership. The third is about capacity, and it is the one museums prefer, because it can be answered with a building: whether the receiving institution is able to conserve, insure and display what it asks for. Directors who answer the first question with the third are changing the subject, and the change is usually noticed. What has shifted over the last decade is not the law, which moves slowly, but the burden of explanation. A museum that once needed only to say that an object had been in its collection since 1897 is now expected to say how it got there, and a surprising number of institutions have discovered that they cannot. The files were never kept, or were kept and never read, and an acquisition that nobody had questioned for a hundred years turns out to rest on a single sentence in a dealer's letter.

The department store was not a bigger shop. It was a different idea about what a shop was for, and the idea arrived all at once in the second half of the nineteenth century. Before it, a customer entered a shop having already decided what to buy, asked the price, and expected to bargain over it. The department store abolished all three habits. Goods were marked with a fixed price, so that no negotiation was possible and none was needed; they were arranged so that a customer could walk among them without being approached by anybody; and entry committed the visitor to buying nothing at all. What was being sold, in other words, was partly the freedom to look. That freedom was profitable, because it produced purchases nobody had intended to make, and it was socially significant, because it gave middle-class women a public place they could enter alone without comment, which almost nothing else in the city did. The decline of these stores is commonly blamed on the internet, which is too late by half a century. They were already losing to the specialist chain and to the car, which made a site outside the city as easy to reach as the middle of it and so removed the one advantage the middle had. What the internet took was the last thing that remained theirs, which was the ability to hold an enormous range of goods in a single place. A building can hold a hundred thousand items. A warehouse that no customer ever sees can hold ten million.

Copyright was invented as a bargain. An author was granted a monopoly for a limited time, and in exchange the work would afterwards belong to everybody. The first English statute set the term at fourteen years, renewable once, and the arithmetic behind it was not sentimental: fourteen years was thought long enough to reward the writing and short enough not to lock up the culture. Every extension since has been argued for on the first half of that bargain and has quietly weakened the second. The difficulty with a long term is not that it enriches authors, most of whom are dead before it expires, but that it makes a vast number of works unusable without making them available. A book still in copyright whose publisher has vanished and whose author cannot be traced may not lawfully be reprinted, digitised or quoted at length, and it is not in print either. Libraries hold millions of such works. They are protected against a use that nobody is proposing, and the protection costs precisely what it protects. Defenders of long terms reply that the alternative punishes the successful, and where a work is still earning they are right. But most works earn nothing after a decade, and a term designed for the exceptions governs everything else. The public domain, when a work at last reaches it, turns out to be productive in ways that are hard to predict and easy to underestimate: editions, translations, adaptations and teaching uses appear within a year of a copyright expiring, because they had been waiting for it.

Historians who argue that childhood was invented are not claiming that people once failed to notice that children are small. They are making a narrower and more interesting claim: that the idea of childhood as a separate condition, with its own clothes, its own books, its own law and its own moral rules, is recent and can be dated. In much of Europe before the eighteenth century a child of seven was dressed as a small adult, worked alongside adults, was tried in the same court and was not thought to need a different kind of literature, because there was none. What changed was not affection. Parents who buried half their children grieved as parents grieve now, and the letters survive to prove it. What changed was the boundary. Schooling lengthened, work moved out of the home, mortality fell, and a stretch of life that had been a short passage into adult labour became a long period with a purpose of its own. The consequences reach a good deal further than the nursery. Almost every modern institution that deals with young people assumes the boundary: compulsory education, the age of criminal responsibility, the law on child labour, the separate courts. Each of them has to decide where childhood ends, and no two of them put the line in the same place, which is the clearest evidence that the line is a decision rather than a discovery. A society argues about the voting age precisely because it has already agreed that there is something there to argue about.

A string quartet needs four players and takes as long to perform as it did two hundred years ago. A factory that made a hundred chairs a week then makes many thousands now. This difference looks like a curiosity and explains a great deal about which things become cheaper and which do not. Where output per worker rises, wages can rise without prices rising with them. Where it cannot rise, because the work itself is the thing being bought, wages still have to keep pace with the rest of the economy or nobody will do the job. The result is that a concert ticket, a school place, a haircut and an hour of nursing all become more expensive relative to manufactured goods, decade after decade, without anybody anywhere being inefficient. This is not a failure. It is the arithmetic of a society growing richer, and the rising price is the sign that it is. The mistake is to treat these services as though they were badly run factories and to look for the savings a factory would find. There are none of the usual kind, because the labour is not a cost attached to the product; it is the product. What can be decided is how much of it a society buys and who pays for it. A country that wants the same number of teachers in fifty years will have to spend a rising share of its income on them, and the argument about whether to do so is a political one that no measure of productivity is going to settle.

questions.why: Parça sürenin ardındaki hesabı verir ve bunun duygusal değil, iki yönlü bir denge olduğunu söyler.
questions.trap_note: Süreyi yazarın ömrüne bağlar; parça ise ödül ile kültürün serbest kalması arasındaki dengeden söz eder.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the works most damaged by a long term are those which ----.

options.o1: nobody is trying to sell and nobody may lawfully copy
options.o2: are still earning a substantial income for their owners
options.o3: were published before the first English statute was passed
options.o4: libraries have already digitised without asking anybody
options.o5: have been translated into more than one language

questions.why: Parçanın tarif ettiği durum tam olarak budur: yayıncısı yok olmuş, yazarı bulunamayan, basılmayan ama kopyalanması da yasak olan kitap.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın 'burada haklılar' dediği durumu seçer; kazanmaya devam eden yapıtlar sorunun değil, istisnanın örneğidir.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that new editions and translations appearing within a year of a copyright's expiry show that ----.

options.o1: those uses had been held back rather than being absent
options.o2: the expiry of a copyright creates demand where there had been none
options.o3: publishers had been waiting for the author of the work to die
options.o4: translations are more profitable than original works are
options.o5: the public domain is chiefly of use to scholars

questions.why: Parça son sözcüğüyle açıklar: bu kullanımlar 'bekliyordu', yani talep vardı ve engellenmişti.
questions.trap_note: Bekleyen talebi yeni doğmuş talep sanır; parçanın 'because they had been waiting' ifadesi bunu dışlar.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: Successive extensions have kept the reward copyright promised and quietly dropped the return the public was promised.
options.o2: Copyright ought to be abolished, since most works earn nothing at all after a decade.
options.o3: Authors are rarely still alive to enjoy the protection the law gives their work.
options.o4: Libraries are the institutions most inconvenienced by the present state of the law.
options.o5: The first English copyright statute was better drafted than any that followed it.

questions.why: Parça boyunca izlenen şey pazarlığın iki yarısıdır: ödül korunmuş, kamuya dönüş sürekli ertelenmiştir.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın savunmadığı uç sonuca atlar; metin süreyi tartışır, telif hakkının kendisini değil.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that the surviving letters are mentioned in order to ----.

options.o1: rule out a change of feeling as the explanation
options.o2: show that parents once felt rather less than parents feel now
options.o3: date the moment at which childhood was invented
options.o4: prove that mortality among children was extremely high
options.o5: describe the kind of literature children were given

questions.why: Mektuplar 'değişen şey sevgi değildi' savının kanıtı olarak getirilir ve bir açıklamayı elemeye yarar.
questions.trap_note: Mektupların gösterdiğinin tersini söyler; metin onları tam da bu yanlış anlamayı önlemek için anar.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a seven-year-old in seventeenth-century Europe ----.

options.o1: was treated as a smaller adult rather than as a different kind of person
options.o2: was thought too young to be held responsible for anything at all
options.o3: was taught from books written especially for children
options.o4: worked only in households that could not afford servants
options.o5: was dressed differently from adults on formal occasions

questions.why: Giyim, iş ve mahkeme üçü de aynı yöne işaret eder: ayrı bir kategori değil, küçültülmüş bir yetişkin.
questions.trap_note: Bugünün ceza ehliyeti anlayışını geçmişe taşır; parça aynı mahkemede yargılandığını söyler.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the boundary of childhood moved because ----.

options.o1: schooling lengthened, work left the home and fewer children died
options.o2: parents came to feel more strongly about their children than before
options.o3: the law created separate courts for those under a certain age
options.o4: books written for children became widely available at last
options.o5: societies began to argue about the age at which one may vote

questions.why: Parça üç nedeni arka arkaya sayar ve bunların çocukluğu kısa bir geçişten uzun bir döneme çevirdiğini söyler.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın açıkça dışladığı açıklamayı seçer: 'değişen şey sevgi değildi' denmektedir.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: Childhood is a boundary societies drew rather than a fact they noticed, and the institutions built on it still cannot agree where it lies.
options.o2: People in earlier centuries cared a good deal less about their children than people do today.
options.o3: Compulsory education did more than any other reform to change the lives of the young.
options.o4: The age of criminal responsibility ought to be the same in every country.
options.o5: Literature written for children appeared later than any other kind of writing.

questions.why: Parça iki şeyi birlikte kurar: sınırın çizilmiş olması ve kurumların onu aynı yere koyamaması.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın baştan reddettiği okumadır; tarihçilerin savı sevginin değil, sınırın değiştiğidir.

questions.stem: According to the passage, wages in services whose output cannot rise must still go up because ----.

options.o1: otherwise nobody would be willing to do the work at all
options.o2: otherwise the services would come to be run as badly as factories
options.o3: the price of manufactured goods keeps on falling
options.o4: governments require them to do so by law
options.o5: the number of people wanting these services keeps growing

questions.why: Parça gerekçeyi doğrudan verir: ücretler ekonominin geri kalanına ayak uydurmazsa o işi yapan kalmaz.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın yönetim benzetmesini gerekçe sanır; fabrika karşılaştırması bir hata uyarısıdır, bir neden değil.

questions.stem: It is clear from the passage that the rising relative price of a haircut ----.

options.o1: is evidence that the rest of the economy has become more productive
options.o2: is evidence that barbers have grown less efficient than they were
options.o3: has been caused chiefly by the rents that barbers have to pay
options.o4: could be reversed by reorganising the way the work is done
options.o5: matters rather less than the rising price of manufactured goods

questions.why: Göreli fiyat artışı, kimse verimsizleşmeden, ekonominin geri kalanının verimlenmesinden doğar.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın 'kimsenin verimsiz olmadığı' vurgusunu tersine çevirir; artışı berberin kusuru sayar.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that looking for a factory's kind of saving in a hospital ----.

options.o1: means cutting the very thing the hospital exists to provide
options.o2: is the only way of keeping the hospital's costs under control
options.o3: has been tried and has reduced costs quite considerably
options.o4: would work well enough if the hospital were better managed
options.o5: is what accounts for the present shortage of nurses

questions.why: Parça emeğin ürüne eklenen bir maliyet değil, ürünün kendisi olduğunu söyler; oradan yapılacak tasarruf ürünü kesmektir.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın hata dediği yaklaşımı tek çözüm olarak sunar; metin tam da bu yaklaşımın yanlışlığını anlatır.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.o1: Services made out of human time necessarily cost more as a society grows richer, and what is left to decide is political rather than managerial.
options.o2: Public services have become expensive because they are managed less efficiently than private firms.
options.o3: Productivity in manufacturing has risen a great deal faster than anybody had predicted.
options.o4: Governments will be unable to employ the same number of teachers fifty years from now.
options.o5: The price of a concert ticket is the clearest single measure of a country's wealth.

questions.why: Parça önce mekanizmayı kurar, sonra geriye kalan sorunun siyasi olduğunu ve verimlilik ölçümüyle çözülemeyeceğini söyler.
questions.trap_note: Parçanın adıyla uyardığı hatayı yapar: bu hizmetleri kötü işletilen fabrikalar gibi okur.

dialogue: In about a third of cases, no. The file gives us a dealer's name and a year, and nothing at all between that year and the ground the object came out of.
And what do you do with the third?
We publish what we have and say plainly what we do not have. It is not a satisfying answer, but an honest gap is worth more than a confident sentence nobody can check.

options.o1: Can you always establish where an object in your collection came from?
options.o2: Do you publish the files of the objects whose origins are disputed?
options.o3: How many objects has the museum returned in the last ten years?
options.o4: Were most of these objects bought from dealers or excavated by the museum?
options.o5: Does the law oblige you to investigate how an object was acquired?

questions.why: İkinci replik 'vakaların üçte birinde hayır' diyerek bir yeterlilik sorusunu yanıtlar ve ardından dosyanın neden yetmediğini anlatır.
questions.trap_note: Yayımlama dördüncü replikte geçer, ama ikinci repliğin 'hayır'ı yayımlamaya değil, kaynağı saptayabilmeye verilmiş bir yanıttır.

dialogue: You argue that the department store was killed by the car rather than by the computer.
Half a century before the computer, yes. Once a family could drive, a site outside the city was as easy to reach as the middle of it, and being in the middle was the whole of the advantage.
It took the last one: holding an enormous range of goods under a single roof. A building can hold a hundred thousand things. A warehouse nobody ever visits can hold ten million.

options.o1: Then what did the internet take, if that advantage had gone already?
options.o2: So the internet had no effect on these stores at all?
options.o3: How long did the out-of-town stores go on growing?
options.o4: Did the city-centre stores not try to move out as well?
options.o5: Were the first of these stores built before the railways?

questions.why: Yanıt 'It took the last one' diye başlar: internetin neyi aldığı sorulmuş olmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Yanıt internetin bir şey aldığını söyler; hiç etkisi olmadığını öne süren bir soruyla çelişir.

dialogue: Your library holds two million books that are in copyright and out of print. What may you actually do with them?
Almost nothing. We may lend the physical copy to one reader at a time. We may not digitise it and we may not reprint it.
Even where the publisher no longer exists and the author cannot be traced?

options.o1: Especially then. There is nobody left to give permission, so the answer is permanently no.
options.o2: In that case the work passes into the public domain and we may do as we like with it.
options.o3: We approach the publisher's successor, who usually agrees within a few weeks.
options.o4: Those are the books we digitise first, since nobody is left to object.
options.o5: The law was amended some years ago precisely to deal with that difficulty.

questions.why: Sorunun vurgusu 'even where' üzerindedir: izin verecek kimsenin kalmaması durumu daha da kilitler.
questions.trap_note: Sahipsizliği kamuya geçişle karıştırır; süre dolmadıkça yapıt kamu malı olmaz.

dialogue: When you say childhood was invented, people hear you saying that parents used to love their children less.
That childhood became a separate condition, with its own clothes, its own books and its own law. A boy of seven in 1600 wore what his father wore and was tried in the same court.

options.o1: That is not the claim at all, and the letters that survive show the opposite.
options.o2: That is the claim, and the letters that survive from the period support it.
options.o3: Parents in that period had a great many more children than they do now.
options.o4: The word childhood itself does not appear before the eighteenth century.
options.o5: Historians disagree with one another about the whole of this question.

questions.why: Sunucunun sözünü bir yanlış anlama olarak aktarması ve ardından 'öyleyse iddia nedir' diye sorması, arada bir reddetmeyi gerektirir.
questions.trap_note: İddiayı kabul eder; oysa bir sonraki replikteki 'öyleyse iddia nedir' sorusu ancak bir reddetmeden sonra anlamlıdır.

dialogue: You say a school cannot be made more productive in the way that a factory can.
Not without changing what it is selling. The hour a teacher spends with a class is not a cost attached to the lesson. It is the lesson.
Then a society that wants the same number of teachers in fifty years will have to spend a rising share of what it earns on them. Whether it wants to is a political question, not an economic one.

options.o1: So the price of that hour is bound to go on rising?
options.o2: So the number of teachers is bound to go on falling?
options.o3: Is that true of manufacturing as much as it is of teaching?
options.o4: How much has the cost of a school place risen already?
options.o5: Would larger classes not solve the problem straight away?

questions.why: Yanıt 'Then ...' ile bir sonucu kabul edip geliştirir: gelirin artan bir payının öğretmenlere gitmesi, saatin pahalılaşmasının karşılığıdır.
questions.trap_note: Yanıt öğretmen sayısının korunabileceğini varsayar; sayının düşeceğini öne süren bir soruyla bağdaşmaz.

questions.stem: Nowhere in the file is there any indication of how the object reached the dealer who sold it.

options.o1: The file contains nothing whatever to show how the object came into the hands of the dealer who sold it.
options.o2: There is one indication in the file of how the object reached the dealer who sold it.
options.o3: The dealer who sold the object refused to say how he had come by it.
options.o4: The file shows that the object reached the dealer through several hands.
options.o5: Nobody has looked in the file to see how the object reached the dealer.

questions.why: Nowhere cümle başına gelince mutlak bir olumsuzluk kurar: dosyada bu konuda hiçbir kayıt yoktur.
questions.trap_note: Mutlak olumsuzluğu tek bir kayda çevirir; 'nowhere' sayı bildirmez, yokluk bildirir.

questions.stem: Rather than compete with the out-of-town stores on price, the old city-centre shops tried to compete on range, and lost.

options.o1: Instead of competing on price with the out-of-town stores, the city-centre shops competed on range and were beaten.
options.o2: Instead of competing on range with the out-of-town stores, the city-centre shops competed on price and were beaten.
options.o3: The city-centre shops competed with the out-of-town stores on both price and range at once.
options.o4: The out-of-town stores offered a wider range than the city-centre shops were able to.
options.o5: Competing on price would have saved the city-centre shops from defeat.

questions.why: Rather than X, Y kalıbında yapılan Y'dir: şehir merkezindeki dükkânlar fiyatla değil, çeşitle yarışmıştır.
questions.trap_note: Yapılanla yapılmayanı değiştirir; kalıbın iki ucu takas edilince olay tersine döner.

questions.stem: So little of the catalogue is still earning anything that the length of the term is irrelevant to all but a handful of titles.

options.o1: Because hardly anything in the catalogue still earns, the length of the term matters to no more than a few titles.
options.o2: Because hardly anything in the catalogue still earns, the length of the term matters to every title in it.
options.o3: A handful of titles earn so much that the length of the term makes no difference to them.
options.o4: Nothing in the catalogue has earned anything since the term was last extended.
options.o5: The catalogue would earn a good deal more if the term were made shorter.

questions.why: So ... that yapısı bir derece-sonuç ilişkisi kurar: kazanç yok denecek kadar azsa süre yalnızca birkaç yapıt için anlamlıdır.
questions.trap_note: Sonucu tersine çevirir; aynı nedenden her yapıt için önemli olduğu sonucunu çıkarır.

questions.stem: Not one of the institutions concerned has been able to say where childhood ends without contradicting another of them.

options.o1: Every one of the institutions concerned, in saying where childhood ends, contradicts at least one of the others.
options.o2: Only one of the institutions concerned has said where childhood ends without contradicting the others.
options.o3: The institutions concerned have agreed among themselves where childhood ends.
options.o4: None of the institutions concerned has been willing to say where childhood ends.
options.o5: Where childhood ends is a question the institutions concerned have never asked.

questions.why: Not one ... without kalıbı çifte olumsuzluk kurar: hepsi bir yaş söylemiştir ve her biri bir başkasıyla çelişmektedir.
questions.trap_note: 'Not one' ifadesini 'yalnızca biri' diye okur; kalıp sayı değil, istisnasızlık bildirir.

questions.stem: A set of minutes is not a record of what was said; it is a record of what the meeting is willing to have said. ---- A remark everybody heard can be left out because nobody wants it repeated, and a decision nobody quite took can appear as a single settled sentence. The document is evidence of something, then, but of the meeting's account of itself rather than of the meeting.

options.o1: The difference is not dishonesty; it is selection.
options.o2: Most organisations now record their meetings in full.
options.o3: Minutes are usually circulated within a few days.
options.o4: The secretary is rarely a participant in the discussion.
options.o5: Long meetings tend to produce the shortest minutes.

questions.why: Boşluktan sonra iki örnek verilir: çıkarılan bir söz ve düzeltilmiş bir karar. Boşluk bunları tek bir kavramda toplamalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Paragrafın savını teknik bir çözümle karşılar; oysa metin kaydın eksikliğinden değil, seçiciliğinden söz eder.

questions.stem: A shoe that costs forty pounds and can be resoled twice is cheaper over ten years than one that costs fifteen and cannot be repaired at all. ---- The calculation is easy and almost nobody makes it, because the money that matters is the money one has this month. A policy that hopes to reduce waste by explaining the arithmetic is therefore addressing the wrong difficulty: what prevents the better purchase is not ignorance but the price on the day.

options.o1: This is no secret, and it is not hard to work out.
options.o2: Most buyers are unaware that resoling is possible at all.
options.o3: Shoes of the second kind have become far more common.
options.o4: Repair shops have closed in most towns over thirty years.
options.o5: Leather lasts longer than the materials that replaced it.

questions.why: Paragrafın sonucu 'engel bilgisizlik değil' olduğuna göre boşluk, hesabın zaten bilindiğini söylemelidir.
questions.trap_note: Paragrafın açıkça reddettiği açıklamayı kurar: sorun bilgisizlik değil, o günkü fiyattır.

questions.stem: The map of a city's underground railway is not a map of the city. ---- Distances are stretched where the stations are close together and compressed where they are far apart, the lines are drawn at angles no surveyor would recognise, and the river is the only thing in the right place. All of this makes the map useless for walking and very good indeed at the one thing it is for, which is telling a passenger where to change.

options.o1: It is a diagram, and it is deliberately wrong about geography.
options.o2: It is drawn to a scale that varies from one district to another.
options.o3: It was first drawn in the 1930s by an engineering draughtsman.
options.o4: Most cities now print a second map for visitors on foot.
options.o5: The colours of the lines are chosen to be easy to tell apart.

questions.why: Boşluktan sonra sayılanların hepsi bilerek yapılmış coğrafi hatalardır; boşluk bu tercihi adlandırmalıdır.
questions.trap_note: Bir ayrıntıyı tanım yerine koyar; ölçeğin değişmesi sonuçtur, haritanın ne olduğu değil.

questions.stem: A footnote is often read as a display of learning, and it is usually the opposite. ---- It tells the reader where the claim above it came from, which is another way of saying that the claim can be checked and, if the source will not bear it, rejected. A book with no notes asks to be believed; a book with notes asks to be examined. The second is the more modest request, though it looks like the prouder one.

options.o1: Its function is to hand the reader a means of disagreeing.
options.o2: Its function is to show how widely the author has read.
options.o3: Notes were once printed in the margin rather than at the foot.
options.o4: Publishers dislike them because they add to the length.
options.o5: Readers of general books almost never look at them.

questions.why: Boşluktan sonraki cümle dipnotun işini açıklar: kaynağı vermek, iddiayı denetlenebilir kılmaktır.
questions.trap_note: Paragrafın 'tam tersi' diyerek dışladığı okumayı seçer; bilgi gösterisi tam da reddedilen açıklamadır.

sentences: An alphabetical index is so ordinary a thing that it is easy to forget somebody had to invent it.
It could not exist before the page number, and the page number could not exist before printing made every copy of a book identical.
Once those two conditions were met, a reader could be told exactly where to look instead of being told to read on until the passage appeared.
Paper had replaced parchment in most European workshops by the fifteenth century.
The index turned the book from something to be read through into something to be consulted.
questions.why: IV. cümle kâğıdın parşömenin yerini almasına geçer; paragrafın kurduğu 'dizin neyi gerektirdi, neyi değiştirdi' zincirinde yeri yoktur.
questions.trap_note: I. cümle bir genel gözlem gibi durur ama paragrafın konusunu açar: sıradan görünen şeyin icat edilmiş olması.

sentences: The first fire brigades in London were paid for by insurance companies and answered only to the houses their own company had insured.
Modern fire engines carry equipment for road accidents as well as for fires.
A house displayed a metal badge showing which company it had paid, and a brigade arriving at a fire insured by a rival would sometimes leave it burning.
The arrangement was defended on the ground that each company protected what it had undertaken to protect.
It ended when the companies themselves concluded that a fire nobody put out does not stay on one side of a wall.
questions.why: II. cümle bugünün itfaiye donanımına geçer; paragraf ise sigortaya bağlı itfaiyenin nasıl kurulup neden bittiğini anlatır.
questions.trap_note: I. cümle uzun bir tarihsel giriş gibi görünür ama paragrafın bütün savı orada kurulan düzenin üzerinedir.

sentences: Nobody knew how to begin a telephone call for the first thirty years of the instrument's existence.
Proposals included 'Ahoy', 'Are you there' and a silence in which the caller waited to be addressed first.
The problem was a real one: two people who could not see each other had no way of establishing which of them should speak.
'Hello', which had until then been a shout used to attract attention at a distance, was pressed into service and settled the question.
Telephone exchanges were operated almost entirely by women from the 1880s onwards.
questions.why: V. cümle santral çalışanlarına geçer; paragrafın konusu konuşmaya nasıl başlanacağının çözülmesidir.
questions.trap_note: I. cümle abartılı bir iddia gibi durur ama paragrafın çözdüğü sorunu ortaya koyan cümledir.

sentences: The postcard was opposed when it was first proposed, on the ground that a message anybody could read was not a letter at all.
The objection was answered by the price, which was a fraction of what sending a letter cost.
Within a decade the postcard had produced a kind of writing that had not existed before: short, public and unembarrassed.
Postal services in most countries of the period were run by the state rather than by private firms.
What had been an indecency became a convention, and then a form.
questions.why: IV. cümle posta idarelerinin mülkiyetine geçer; paragraf ise kartpostalın itirazı aşıp yeni bir yazı biçimine dönüşmesini anlatır.
questions.trap_note: II. cümle konu dışı bir ayrıntı sanılır; oysa itirazın nasıl aşıldığını söyleyen halkadır.

sentences: The first public reading rooms admitted anybody who could produce a letter of introduction from somebody already admitted.
The books themselves were chained to the shelves in many of the earliest collections.
The rule was not written in order to exclude the poor, but that is what it did, since a letter of introduction is a thing one's acquaintances can supply.
Removing it took thirty years and was resisted by readers who expected the room to fill with people unlike themselves.
The room did fill, and the objection was quietly dropped rather than answered.
questions.why: II. cümle kitapların zincirlenmesine geçer; paragrafın konusu okuma odasına kimin girebildiğidir.
questions.trap_note: IV. cümle itirazı anlattığı için konudan sapma sanılır; oysa kuralın kaldırılışı paragrafın vardığı yerdir.

vocabulary: excavation (the ground the object came out of)
promise (the return the public was promised)
saving (the savings a factory would find)
